The supplied October 2026 course paper compared a nearest-centroid classifier and a fixed rule on artificially altered pulse recordings. This experiment does not validate diagnosis, emergency detection, or wearable measurement accuracy.
Archived paper results: ML F1 0.7914; balanced accuracy 0.4909; specificity 0.1951. The rule had balanced accuracy 0.6006. These results were not rerun by this Android app.
No classifier is used on your personal records. Smartwatch import, live sensors, clinical alerts, and cloud synchronization are not included in this version.

Research demo: artificial disturbances in recorded pulse signals

This follows the course paper. It checks whether two methods can recognise deliberate changes added to recorded pulse values. It does not read your pulse, measure heart rate, or diagnose anything, and it never touches your health records.

The paper trains on pulse1.csv and pulse3.csv and tests on the held-out pulse5.csv from Pathak et al. (2020). Download the three files on this phone from the addresses below, then import each one. One value per line; for files with two columns the last number is used.
Synthetic signals are computer-generated practice waves, not real recordings. Use them only to try the screen; they do not reproduce the paper.
That file could not be read. It needs at least 256 numeric values.
The experiment could not run with these recordings.
The first training recording needs at least 1,024 values for the noise test.

Windows of 256 values move 128 at a time. Each window gives one unchanged copy and four altered copies: added noise, isolated spikes, a 48-point flat line, and a linear baseline drift (4 altered : 1 unchanged). Six features are computed per window. The nearest-centroid classifier is fitted on the training recordings only; the fixed rule flags a window when more than 0.12 of its successive differences are exactly zero.
These results use synthetic practice signals, not the recordings in the paper.

Disturbance strengths are not stated in the paper, so this app uses: noise 0.35 × window SD, 3 spikes of 4 × SD, a 48-point flat line, and a drift of 1 × SD; seed 47. The flat-line rule does not depend on these strengths. The classifier result can differ from the archived run.
Grey: original values. Green: values after the program changed them.
This copy was %1$s. ML says %2$s; the rule says %3$s.

Gaussian noise is added to the first 1,024 values of training recording 1 at eight scales (0 to 1 × its SD), 30 draws per scale, seed 20261023. The SD of successive differences measures how rough the wave becomes.
Roughness rises from %1$s with no noise to %2$s at the largest noise scale
Green line: this run. Outlined dots: Table 2 of the paper.

The labels only say which windows a program changed; they are not expert artifact labels. Three recordings, overlapping windows, an unknown sampling rate and a 4:1 class imbalance limit what the numbers mean. Nothing here estimates heart rate, detects disease or replaces medical care.

Data: N. Pathak, A. Mukherjee and S. Misra, Reconfigure and Reuse: Interoperable Wearables for Healthcare IoT, IEEE INFOCOM 2020, doi 10.1109/INFOCOM41043.2020.9155398; Reconfigure-Reuse-Dataset on GitHub.
